doc.title: Ignacio Berroa interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 22, 2021 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Stereotyped as a Latino percussionist, not a straight-ahead player
summary: He describes being boxed in as a conga or timbales player, which limits work on his own projects; Rowe praises his trio album.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Well I’m glad you said that because I actually had a question for you and you are in a large sense a percussionist who came from Cuba. Has that resulted in people making assumptions about you? For instance, “Oh yeah, Ignacio, does he play the timbales or the congas or the bongos?”

Yeah it has been that way, especially with the people in the industry. My peers, my colleagues, those that know me from the days of the Dizzy Gillespie days, those who have followed my career, those who know my albums, my three albums, those who have seen me playing in jam sessions, they know, and I consider myself I’m a straight ahead jazz player. But what happens? It has nothing to do with being American, being Cuban, being from Senegal, Senegalese, or from Peru. It is human nature. And here in the United States, and maybe it happens in other countries, if you are a foreigner, and especially in my case if you are Cuban everybody, when they think about Cuba they think about conga drums. Conga drums, timbales. I’m a Latino. I’m a Latino. So because I’m a Latino they box me into that category. I’m a Latino. “Oh Ignacio, man, yeah.” Even if they’re going to say that I’m a good, that I can play straight ahead jazz and say, “Oh Ignacio, yeah man, he can play straight ahead jazz. But that Afro-Cuban thing he plays man.” That, you know, it is something that I don’t think they do it on purpose. It’s a stereotype. I’m Cuban, and for that reason, in my opinion, I haven’t been able to work much with my own projects because for promoters, for people in the industry, and I understand that, they want to put seats — they want to fill those seats. And the best way to do that is announcing, “Ignacio Berroa, his Afro-Cuban project.” And a Cuban congero, Ignacio Berroa. A Cuban timbale player. That’s the stereotype unfortunately. Once again, a lot of my peers and my colleagues I feel happy I have gained their respect and they respect me for what I have done, meaning coming to this country and being able to absorb the vocabulary and play their music, let’s put it this way, at the highest level possible. For those who call the shots in many cases, and when I’m able to do anything, they box me in. I’m a Latino and Ignacio — oh yes, — if Ignacio wants to play straight ahead, who wants to see a Cuban guy play straight ahead? Come on. Right? That type of thing. I have lived through that. I have been here for 41 years and that’s the way it has been in my case. Why? Once again, people expect me to play conga drums, timbales, cowbell. They want to see Desi Arnaz.

All right. Well you’ve been able to get out of the box on the projects you’ve done. And the one you sent me, “Straight Ahead from Havana,” when I listen to it I’m fascinated by the compositions for one thing, and how interactive the whole trio is with all the accents and the, it’s complex. And you’re right there with all of that. You’re very active on this record, and I’m not sure if I have a question here except that I admire it and it’s wonderful music.
